title: Photosynthesis
tagline: Raw materials and requirements, light and dark reactions, chloroplast structure, classic experiments and the carbon cycle.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class X Biology syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: Photosynthesis is the process that turns light energy into the chemical energy on which almost every food chain depends: 6CO2 + 6H2O in the presence of chlorophyll and light gives C6H12O6 + 6O2. This chapter covers the requirements and raw materials, the two stages inside the chloroplast — the light-dependent reactions that split water and produce ATP and NADPH, and the light-independent reactions that fix carbon dioxide into sugar — the structure of the chloroplast that houses them, and the classic experiments (iodine test, variegated leaf, carbon dioxide removal, oxygen evolution) that establish each requirement. The chapter closes by placing photosynthesis inside the carbon cycle.

facts.label: Two stages
facts.value: Light reactions (thylakoids) produce ATP/NADPH; dark reactions (stroma) fix CO2 into sugar

facts.label: Gas exchange
facts.value: CO2 enters and O2 leaves through the stomata

blocks.text: Photosynthesis occurs in the chloroplasts of green cells, chiefly the palisade mesophyll of leaves. It requires light energy, chlorophyll, carbon dioxide and water. Carbon dioxide enters through the stomata and dissolves in the water film of the cell walls; water is drawn up from the roots in the transpiration stream. Chlorophyll absorbs light — most strongly in the red and blue regions — and its green reflection is why leaves look green. The products are glucose and oxygen; the oxygen comes from the splitting of water, not from carbon dioxide, which was proved by isotopic tracing. Some glucose is converted to starch for storage and to cellulose for cell walls, and excess is translocated as sucrose to roots, fruits and growing points.

items.meaning: Conversion of light energy into chemical energy stored as carbohydrate, using CO2 and water.
Green pigment in chloroplasts that absorbs light energy; chlorophyll a is the chief photosynthetic pigment.
Double-membrane organelle with grana (stacks of thylakoids) and stroma where the two stages occur.
Iodine solution turns blue-black in the presence of starch — the standard photosynthesis indicator.

items: Raw materials: carbon dioxide (from air via stomata) and water (from soil via xylem).
Conditions: light energy and chlorophyll.
Products: glucose and oxygen; oxygen is released to the air.
Glucose is used for respiration, converted to starch for storage, changed to cellulose and proteins, or turned to sucrose for transport.
Only cells containing chloroplasts can photosynthesise — guard cells can, root cells cannot.

items.text: Variegated leaf stained with iodine: only the previously green (chlorophyll-containing) areas turn blue-black.
items.note: The white regions had light and CO2 but no chlorophyll — proving chlorophyll is essential.

items.text: Water plant (Hydrilla) in sunlight gives a steady stream of bubbles — oxygen evolved during photosynthesis.
items.note: Counting bubbles under different light colours shows red and blue light are most effective.

blocks.text: Photosynthesis proceeds in two linked stages inside the chloroplast. The light-dependent reactions take place on the thylakoid membranes of the grana: chlorophyll absorbs light, water is split (photolysis) releasing oxygen, hydrogen and electrons; the energy captured is used to make ATP and to reduce NADP to NADPH. The light-independent reactions — the Calvin cycle — occur in the stroma and do not need light directly: carbon dioxide is attached to a five-carbon compound and, using the ATP and NADPH from the first stage, is reduced in steps to a three-carbon sugar, from which glucose and other organic molecules are built. The two stages are coupled: the light reactions supply the reducing power and energy that the dark reactions consume, which is why overall photosynthesis stops in the dark even though the dark reactions themselves need no light.

items: Light reactions: thylakoid membranes; water split; O2 released; ATP and NADPH produced.
Dark reactions (Calvin cycle): stroma; CO2 fixed and reduced to sugar using ATP and NADPH.
Photolysis: 2H2O -> 4H+ + 4e- + O2 — the source of released oxygen.
Carbon dioxide is 'fixed' by combining with a 5-carbon acceptor (RuBP) in the stroma.
No light -> no ATP/NADPH -> Calvin cycle stops; both stages are therefore light-dependent overall.
Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light best and reflects green — the reason for leaf colour.

items.text: Plant kept in continuous dark loses starch after a few days — stored starch is used up by respiration.
items.note: This destarching step is what makes the later iodine test valid.

items.text: Isotope tracing with O-18 shows the released oxygen comes from H2O, not CO2.
items.note: The classic experiment that overturned the assumption that oxygen came from carbon dioxide.

items.meaning: Splitting of water by light energy, releasing oxygen, hydrogen ions and electrons.
Light-independent reactions in the stroma fixing CO2 into carbohydrate.
Stacks of thylakoids (light reactions) / fluid matrix (dark reactions) of the chloroplast.
Removing stored starch by keeping a plant in darkness before a photosynthesis experiment.

blocks.text: Each requirement is proved by removing exactly one factor while holding the others constant. The starch test: destarch a plant, expose a leaf partly covered with black paper to light, then test with iodine — only the exposed area turns blue-black, proving light is necessary. The chlorophyll test: a variegated leaf shows starch only where it was green. The carbon dioxide test: a potted plant is enclosed with soda lime (which absorbs CO2) and, after exposure to light, its leaves test negative for starch while a control plant in ordinary air tests positive. The oxygen test: aquatic plants bubble in light, and the gas relights a glowing splint. In every case the control plant is essential — it proves the treatment, not the plant's health, caused the difference.

items: Always destarch first — otherwise pre-existing starch ruins the comparison.
Cover part of a leaf with black paper: the covered part gets light but no starch result — light is required.
Soda lime removes CO2: no CO2, no starch — carbon dioxide is a raw material.
Variegated leaf: no chlorophyll, no starch — chlorophyll is required.
Boil the leaf in alcohol (water bath) to remove chlorophyll before adding iodine.
Control = identical plant without the single changed factor.

items.text: Iodine test: decolourised leaf + iodine turns blue-black where starch is present; stays brown-yellow where absent.
items.note: Alcohol must be heated on a water bath, never a naked flame — ethanol is highly flammable.

items.text: Soda lime experiment: plant with soda lime shows no blue-black colour; control without it does.
items.note: One variable changed, everything else identical — the structure of a valid experiment.

blocks.text: Carbon cycles continuously between atmosphere, producers, consumers and decomposers. Photosynthesis draws carbon dioxide out of the air and fixes it as glucose; respiration by plants, animals and microbes returns it as carbon dioxide. When organisms die, decayers decompose their remains, releasing CO2; combustion of fossil fuels and wood returns carbon that has been locked away for millions of years. In this balance, photosynthesis is the only major entry route for atmospheric carbon into the living world, and the oceans act as a large reservoir, dissolving and releasing CO2. Human combustion has shifted the balance — releasing stored carbon faster than photosynthesis recaptures it — which is why deforestation and burning both raise atmospheric CO2 levels.

items: Carbon enters the biosphere ONLY through photosynthesis.
Respiration (plants, animals, decomposers) returns CO2 continuously.
Fossil fuel combustion releases ancient stored carbon at an unnatural rate.
Oceans dissolve CO2 — a buffer reservoir, but acidification is a consequence.
Decomposition and decay return the carbon locked in dead matter.
Trees act as carbon sinks; cutting them both stops uptake and releases stored carbon if burned.

items.text: A forest fire releases in days the carbon a forest accumulated over years — net CO2 source.
items.note: Burning converts fixed carbon back to atmospheric CO2 almost instantly.

items.text: Peat and coal store carbon from ancient swamps — photosynthesis of the Carboniferous, released today by combustion.
items.note: Fossil fuels are photosynthesis that waited hundreds of millions of years.

figures.caption: Figure: Structure of a chloroplast
figures.description: Double outer membrane; stacks of thylakoids (grana) where light reactions occur; fluid stroma where the Calvin cycle runs; chlorophyll embedded in the thylakoid membranes.

figures.caption: Figure: The overall process and gas exchange
figures.description: CO2 enters and O2 exits through stomata; water rises in the xylem; light is captured by chlorophyll; glucose is made in the stroma and transported as sucrose or stored as starch.

keyPoints: 6CO2 + 6H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2 in presence of light and chlorophyll.
Requirements: light, chlorophyll, CO2 and water; products: glucose and oxygen.
Released oxygen comes from the splitting of water (photolysis), not CO2.
Light reactions on thylakoids produce ATP and NADPH and release O2; Calvin cycle in the stroma fixes CO2 into sugar.
Iodine turns blue-black with starch — the standard photosynthesis test.
Experiments must destarch the plant, change one variable and include a control.
No CO2 (soda lime) or no chlorophyll (variegated leaf) means no starch.
Photosynthesis is the entry point of carbon into the carbon cycle; respiration and combustion return it.
examFocus: Experiment questions need four elements: destarching, the single variable, the control, and the iodine result — missing the control loses marks consistently.
Write the equation with conditions above the arrow: light and chlorophyll, not heat or enzymes alone.
Light versus dark reactions: state LOCATION, INPUTS and OUTPUTS of each — the coupling through ATP/NADPH earns the top marks.
For oxygen source, quote the water-splitting evidence rather than reasoning from the equation alone.

vocabulary.meaning: Light-driven splitting of water releasing O2, H+ and electrons.
Light-independent CO2 fixation in the stroma.
Removing stored starch in darkness before testing.
Fluid matrix / thylakoid stacks of the chloroplast.
Reservoir accumulating carbon, e.g. a growing forest.
Green pigment absorbing light energy for photosynthesis.

questions.prompt: The oxygen released during photosynthesis comes from:
questions.explanation: Photolysis splits water during the light reactions; isotope tracing with O-18 proved the released O2 derives from H2O, not CO2.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming oxygen comes from CO2 because CO2 contains more oxygen — the bonds of water are the ones broken by light.

questions.prompt: In which part of the chloroplast do the light-dependent reactions occur?
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll and the electron transport machinery lie in the thylakoid membranes; the stroma hosts the Calvin cycle.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing stroma — it is where CO2 is fixed, not where light is captured.

questions.prompt: A plant enclosed with soda lime and exposed to light shows no starch because:
questions.explanation: Without CO2 the Calvin cycle cannot fix carbon, so no glucose and no starch form — proving CO2 is a necessary raw material.
questions.commonMistake: Saying it blocks light — the bottle is transparent; the changed variable is carbon dioxide.

questions.prompt: Iodine solution gives a blue-black colour in the presence of:
questions.explanation: The iodine-starch complex is blue-black; this is why leaves are destarched and then tested with iodine in photosynthesis experiments.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing glucose — reducing-sugar tests (Fehling/Benedict) detect glucose; iodine detects the stored form.

questions.prompt: Why must a plant be destarched before a photosynthesis experiment?
options: To remove starch stored from earlier photosynthesis so new starch can be attributed to the treatment
To wash dust from the stomata
questions.answer: To remove starch stored from earlier photosynthesis so new starch can be attributed to the treatment
questions.explanation: Pre-existing starch would turn iodine blue-black everywhere, masking the effect of the variable being tested.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking destarching increases sensitivity — it prevents false positives, not improves detection.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the overall equation for photosynthesis is 6CO2 + 6H2O --(light, chlorophyll)--> ________ + ________.
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide and water are converted to glucose and oxygen; the conditions must be written above the arrow.
questions.commonMistake: Forgetting the conditions — an equation without light and chlorophyll above the arrow is incomplete.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: chlorophyll absorbs light most strongly in the ________ and ________ regions and reflects green light.
questions.explanation: Absorption peaks in red and blue wavelengths drive photosynthesis; the unabsorbed green light is reflected, giving leaves their colour.
questions.commonMistake: Saying green light is absorbed most — it is reflected, which is precisely why leaves look green.

questions.prompt: Describe an experiment to show that light is necessary for photosynthesis, including the control.
questions.answer: Destarch a potted plant by keeping it in darkness for 48 hours. Then cover part of one leaf with black paper (permeable to neither light nor gas on the covered strip) and expose the plant to bright sunlight for several hours. Kill the leaf in boiling water, decolourise it in alcohol heated on a water bath, wash and add iodine solution. The exposed area turns blue-black; the covered area stays brown-yellow, showing starch formed only where light reached. The uncovered part of the same leaf acts as the control, receiving light under otherwise identical conditions.
questions.explanation: Destarching removes old starch; the covered strip and exposed area differ only in light, so the difference in iodine response is attributable to light.
questions.commonMistake: Using a different plant as the control instead of two areas of the same leaf — less convincing because more variables differ.

questions.prompt: Explain the roles of the light reactions and the dark reactions, stating where each occurs and how they depend on each other.
questions.answer: Light reactions occur on the thylakoid membranes of the grana: chlorophyll absorbs light, water is split by photolysis releasing oxygen, and the captured energy is used to produce ATP and NADPH. Dark reactions (the Calvin cycle) occur in the stroma: carbon dioxide is fixed and, using the ATP and NADPH from the light reactions, reduced to carbohydrate. The stages depend on each other because the Calvin cycle cannot run without the ATP and NADPH supplied by the light reactions — so although the dark reactions need no light directly, overall photosynthesis stops in the dark when the supply of ATP and NADPH is cut off.
questions.explanation: Each stage needs location, inputs and outputs, plus the coupling statement explaining why 'dark reactions' still depend on light overall.
questions.commonMistake: Saying dark reactions happen at night — they run whenever ATP and NADPH are available, including in daylight.

questions.prompt: Describe the carbon cycle, naming the processes that remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and those that return it, and explain how human activity has altered the balance.
questions.answer: Carbon dioxide leaves the atmosphere mainly by photosynthesis, when green plants fix it into glucose; some dissolves in oceans. It returns to the atmosphere by respiration of plants, animals and microorganisms; by decomposition of dead organic matter by saprophytic bacteria and fungi; by combustion of wood and fossil fuels; and by volcanic and oceanic release. Human activity upsets the balance in two ways: burning fossil fuels releases carbon stored over millions of years far faster than it was fixed, and deforestation removes the photosynthetic sink that would absorb the released CO2. The net effect is rising atmospheric carbon dioxide, which enhances the greenhouse effect and drives climate change.
questions.explanation: Full marks need both directions listed with named processes plus the two human impacts — release rate increased AND uptake decreased.
questions.commonMistake: Naming only burning as the human impact — deforestation reducing uptake is the equally required half.

questions.prompt: A variegated leaf (green centre, white margin) is destarched, illuminated and tested with iodine. Only the centre turns blue-black. What does this show, and what must be controlled?
questions.answer: The centre contained chlorophyll and produced starch; the white margin lacked chlorophyll and did not, although it received identical light, carbon dioxide and water. This shows chlorophyll is essential for photosynthesis. To make the conclusion valid, the plant must first be destarched so the blue-black result reflects new starch; all other conditions must be identical for both regions (the marginal area acts as its own control); and a plant kept in the dark throughout should test negative for starch to confirm the iodine test detects only newly formed starch.
questions.explanation: The design exploits one natural variable (chlorophyll presence) within a single leaf, but validity depends on destarching and consistent conditions.
questions.commonMistake: Concluding 'light is unnecessary for the white part' — the correct inference is that chlorophyll is required; light was present everywhere.
